prompt: What must the subnet that holds a VPN gateway be called?
hint: The name is how Azure finds it.

choices.text: `snet-gateway`, by the naming convention
choices.why: A convention is ours; this name is Azure's rule, and a different one fails.

choices.text: `vpng-shop`, the same as the gateway
choices.why: The gateway's name is free; the subnet's is fixed.

choices.text: Anything, as long as it is `/27` or larger
choices.why: Size is a second rule; the name is the first.

choices.text: `GatewaySubnet`, exactly
choices.why: Right. Azure finds the subnet by that name.

prompt: Why does the shop make `GatewaySubnet` a `/27` rather than the smallest size it could get away with?
hint: Who else may need to live there later?

choices.text: Because each tunnel takes one address from the subnet
choices.why: Tunnels use the gateway's public addresses, not the subnet's.

choices.text: Because Azure charges less for a larger subnet
choices.why: Subnets cost nothing at any size.

choices.text: So an ExpressRoute gateway can share it later
choices.why: Right. And growing a small one under a running gateway is a project.

choices.text: So that virtual machines can be placed next to the gateway
choices.why: Nothing else may live in `GatewaySubnet`.

prompt: A gateway is in the default active-standby mode. Microsoft maintains the active instance. What do users of the tunnel notice?
hint: Two instances, one carrying the tunnel.

choices.text: Nothing at all, since both instances carry the tunnel
choices.why: That is active-active. By default only one does.

choices.text: A brief interruption while the standby takes over
choices.why: Right. Active-active removes most of it.

choices.text: An outage of 45 minutes while the gateway is rebuilt
choices.why: 45 minutes is creating a gateway; failover is the standby taking over.

choices.text: Traffic moves to ExpressRoute
choices.why: The shop has no circuit in this design.

prompt: With an active-active gateway and two firewalls in the office, each firewall connected to both instances, how many tunnels are up?
hint: Two times two.

prompt: What is the Basic VPN gateway SKU for?
hint: Microsoft's documentation says it outright.

choices.text: Trying things out
choices.why: Right. Limited features, limited support, never production.

choices.text: Active-active pairs on a budget
choices.why: Basic supports neither active-active nor BGP.

choices.text: Small offices in production
choices.why: Microsoft says it should not be used for production at all.

choices.text: Point-to-site connections only
choices.why: It does site-to-site too; it is just small.

prompt: Five administrators need to reach the hub network from home. Which kind of VPN fits?
hint: One network to another, or one laptop?

choices.text: A site-to-site VPN to each home router
choices.why: That would put five homes' networks into Azure's routing.

choices.text: ExpressRoute with Microsoft peering
choices.why: A circuit is for a building, and weeks to order.

choices.text: None: VPN gateways accept only offices
choices.why: Gateways accept single clients too.

choices.text: Point-to-site, with a client on each laptop
choices.why: Right. And sign-in can go through Entra ID.

prompt: In a site-to-site VPN, what does the local network gateway describe?
hint: Azure's description of the other end.

choices.text: Azure's own gateway in `GatewaySubnet`
choices.why: That is the virtual network gateway, `vpng-shop`.

choices.text: The office's end of the tunnel
choices.why: Right. `lgw-shop-office`, at `203.0.113.10`.

choices.text: The tunnel and its shared key
choices.why: That is the connection, `cn-shop-office`.

choices.text: The DNS server the office uses
choices.why: DNS is lesson 21's subject; this resource is about the far end of the tunnel.

prompt: What did `@secure()` change in the compiled template?
hint: Look at the type the parameter came out with.

choices.text: The parameter's type became `securestring`
choices.why: Right. Resource Manager keeps its value out of the history and the logs.

choices.text: Nothing: decorators are dropped by the compiler
choices.why: This one became the parameter's type.

choices.text: It encrypted the shared key inside the template
choices.why: There is no key in the template to encrypt; it is given at deployment.

choices.text: It made the parameter optional
choices.why: It has no default, so it stays required.

prompt: `leaky.bicep` wrote the shared key as a default value. What did the compiler do?
hint: Was it an error or something milder?

choices.text: Refused to compile it
choices.why: It compiled; the objection was a warning.

choices.text: Removed the value from the template silently
choices.why: It warned, and it changed nothing.

choices.text: Compiled it, with a `secure-parameter-default` warning
choices.why: Right. Nothing stops a deployment unless a pipeline treats warnings as failures.

choices.text: Replaced the key with `newGuid()`
choices.why: `newGuid()` is what the rule allows, not what the compiler writes for you.

prompt: With BGP on, why does the shop's local network gateway list `192.168.255.1/32` and not the office's `192.168.0.0/16`?
hint: Who tells Azure about the office's networks?

choices.text: Because a local network gateway accepts only one address
choices.why: It accepts a list; with BGP, one entry is all it needs.

choices.text: The firewall announces its networks over BGP itself
choices.why: Right. Azure needs only the route to the BGP session.

choices.text: Because `192.168.0.0/16` overlaps the hub's range
choices.why: The hub is `10.0.0.0/16`; nothing overlaps.

choices.text: To keep the office's ranges secret from Azure
choices.why: The firewall announces them over BGP anyway.

prompt: A Bicep resource marked `___` is named without being created, as the hub network is in `vpn.bicep`.
hint: One word after the resource's type.

prompt: Match each resource of `vpn.bicep` to its part in the VPN.
hint: Only one of them is the tunnel.

pairs.right: Azure's description of the office's end
the tunnel, with its shared key

prompt: What does an ExpressRoute circuit travel over?
hint: It never touches one thing.

choices.text: The public internet, in an encrypted tunnel
choices.why: That is a VPN.

choices.text: Microsoft's edge locations, like Front Door
choices.why: Edge locations serve public HTTP traffic; a circuit meets Microsoft at a peering location.

choices.text: A carrier's private network
choices.why: Right. It never crosses the public internet.

choices.text: The paired region's backbone
choices.why: Pairing has nothing to do with how a company reaches Azure.

prompt: What is a circuit's service key, and how is it handled?
hint: Microsoft's documentation says whether it is secret.

choices.text: A password the company keeps from the provider
choices.why: The company gives it to the provider; that is its purpose.

choices.text: A key that encrypts traffic on the circuit
choices.why: The circuit is not encrypted by default, and the key encrypts nothing.

choices.text: The BGP number of Microsoft's routers
choices.why: BGP numbers are separate; the key identifies the circuit.

choices.text: A GUID the company passes to the provider
choices.why: Right. The only thing the three parties exchange, and not a secret.

prompt: The finance system in the office must reach `10.20.3.0/24` over the circuit. Which peering carries it?
hint: Private addresses of your networks.

choices.text: Private peering
choices.why: Right. It reaches the private addresses of your virtual networks.

choices.text: Global Reach
choices.why: The lesson does not use it; it links circuits to each other.

choices.text: Neither: a circuit reaches only Microsoft 365
choices.why: Private peering exists exactly for your networks.

choices.text: Microsoft peering
choices.why: That reaches Microsoft's public services, such as Microsoft 365.

prompt: A company's circuit has both connections ending on one router in its office. Microsoft's routers are both healthy. What has the company lost?
hint: Where is the single point of failure now?

choices.text: Microsoft peering, which needs two routers
choices.why: Peerings are unaffected by where the company ends its connections.

choices.text: Nothing, since Microsoft's side is redundant
choices.why: Redundancy is end to end; the company's end is now one device.

choices.text: The redundancy: one router failing takes both connections down
choices.why: Right. Microsoft's documentation says this compromises the circuit's design.

choices.text: Half the bandwidth, permanently
choices.why: Bandwidth is the circuit's, whatever router ends it.

prompt: Is traffic on an ExpressRoute circuit encrypted?
hint: Private is a statement about the path.

choices.text: Yes, by the carrier, on every circuit
choices.why: Nothing encrypts it by default.

choices.text: Not by default; IPsec or MACsec adds it
choices.why: Right. Private keeps it off the internet, which is a different thing.

choices.text: Yes, with the service key
choices.why: The service key identifies the circuit and encrypts nothing.

choices.text: No, and it cannot be
choices.why: It can: IPsec through it, or MACsec on ExpressRoute Direct.

prompt: Put the steps of getting an ExpressRoute circuit working in order.
hint: Azure first, the carrier in the middle, traffic last.
items: create the circuit resource, naming provider, location and bandwidth
receive the service key from Azure
give the service key to the provider
the provider builds its side and the circuit becomes Provisioned
configure private peering and connect the gateway
trap: Nothing flows until the provider's step is done, and that step is measured in weeks.

prompt: Which of these protect the shop against losing the peering location in São Paulo? Choose all that apply.
hint: A building can fail as a whole.

choices.text: A site-to-site VPN as a backup road
choices.why: Right. It does not go through the peering location at all.

choices.text: The circuit's secondary connection
choices.why: It ends in the same building as the primary.

choices.text: A second circuit at another peering location
choices.why: Right. Campinas, say, with another carrier.

choices.text: A larger bandwidth on the same circuit
choices.why: More capacity in one building is still one building.

choices.text: Making the gateway subnet `/26`
choices.why: The subnet's size changes nothing outside Azure.

prompt: The office adds a new network, `192.168.40.0/24`. The VPN uses BGP. What does somebody have to change on the Azure side?
hint: Who announces the office's networks?

choices.text: Nothing: the firewall announces it over BGP
choices.why: Right. That is what BGP removes: the second person typing the same range.

choices.text: Create a second connection for the new range
choices.why: One connection carries every network BGP announces.

choices.text: Add the range to `lgw-shop-office`'s address space
choices.why: That is how it works without BGP; with it, the firewall announces it.

choices.text: Recreate the gateway with a larger SKU
choices.why: A new range is a route, not a capacity problem.

prompt: A VPN gateway in Azure uses the BGP number ___ unless told otherwise.
hint: Five digits, in the private range.
